rv.q: Van Hove's electrifying staging is like mainlining it all in one million-volt hit.
This is a merciless and resonantly topical vision of the way modern media fragments our attention.
This version of the Oscar-winning Network is an almost total triumph.
Director Ivo van Hove’s staging is the most triumphant demonstration I have seen of his concepts of space, multimedia and audience/performance relationships.
This is a world of constantly roving cameras, all surface, shine and sterility (or if you will, stare-ility).
Ivo van Hove’s electric staging of Network restores at a stroke my faltering esteem for this director.
It’s a magnetic yet weighty performance, with Cranston becoming craggy and wearied before attaining something that seems like grace.

This is theater as assault and battery, and like many of the best current examples of that genre, it’s only an amplification of what you regularly experience in an age when external stimuli outstrip the human ability to process them.
The whole glossy, hectoring, lurid package has an undeniable charge and compulsion.
This production is thrillingly watchable.
They do their best to hold the entire shebang together but often lose out to the sheer sensory cacophony of this production.
Every one of these choices has proved inspirational in a thrilling evening that is closely adapted from the original and combines rich comedy, social commentary and tragedy in a mere two hours.
It is the most successful fusion of live and recorded elements that I have ever seen.
This is one of those rare occasions where a stage play of a successful film, works impressively well...
With Network, Ivo van Hove delivers his most dazzling London production since A View From the Bridge, which transferred to Broadway and won the Belgian director a Tony Award.
Hall's superb adaptation is one of the shining lights of the entire night.

Indeed, pretty much everything the Breaking Bad star (and Broadway Tony winner) does hits the bullseye in what surely constitutes the most impressive British stage debut from an American actor in years.
"Network" can feel like the storyboard of a show, one still lacking life.
But the Oscar-winning film still exists and I'm not sure we needed to revisit it in this form.

Director Ivo Van Hove turns the stage into a mixed media circus dominated by a TV studio with a giant screen, live camera feeds and scurrying technicians. High above the stage, a quartet of men in black perform the accompanying soundtrack live. Dockery and Douglas Henshall as Beale’s friend Max take time to kick their characters into life.
Van Hove manages to rescue the moments of high emotion from ever feeling too sentimental.
But despite the largesse that has been lavished on this production, it is rather two-dimensional and a tad disappointing.

Cranston’s rendition of depressed TV news anchorman Howard Beale who becomes a ratings sensation after calling bullshit on national television (in response to a firing because his ratings were too low) is a theatrical tour de force.

cn.t: Critics largely praise this prescient media satire for van Hove's spectacular staging and Cranston's magnetic performance, though some find the multimedia production gimmicky and the romantic subplot weak.
